headline: High-risk filesystem and network overlap: Continue can write shared workspace files while EMQX exposes broad network egress, creating leakage and conflict risks; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are lower but real.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, so it may ingest attacker-controlled content from shared files or tool outputs. EMQX exposes HTTP API and broad egress, but no direct parsing bridge is documented. The pairwise pathway exists via shared filesystem rather than a proven direct channel, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory
IF EMQX writes content that Continue later opens as trusted instructions
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Disable MCP servers not needed for the task
Require explicit human review of file-based instructions
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent file handoff

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers and has broad network egress; EMQX touches IoT data and also has broad egress. A shared filesystem or copied artifacts could move sensitive workspace data into EMQX-facing outputs or network traffic. The interaction is inferred from profiles, not directly observed, so medium fits.
conditions: IF source code or editor buffers are copied into EMQX inputs
IF either agent forwards shared files over its network egress
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared workspace
Restrict outbound network destinations
Use separate service accounts and credentials
Review logs for accidental payload inclusion
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write filesystem and supports multiple instances with shared state via filesystem. EMQX exposes HTTP API and broad network egress, so both can mutate shared resources if configured against the same files or endpoints. No locking is documented, making overlapping writes plausible in default-like setups.
conditions: IF both agents target the same writable directory
IF EMQX API actions and Continue file edits occur concurrently
mitigations: Assign separate writable directories
Serialize edits with a simple operator checklist
Avoid concurrent runs on the same resource
Snapshot files before each run
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable state

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or file edits that EMQX may consume indirectly through shared files or API payloads. EMQX has HTTP API access and broad egress, so if it acts on Continue's output without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF EMQX treats Continue-produced text or files as authoritative
IF downstream actions are triggered from unverified Continue output
mitigations: Require a human approval step before actions
Validate outputs against a schema
Compare against source-of-truth records
Limit EMQX to read-only mode for test runs
requires-engineering: add verification gates before API actions

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is an IDE assistant handling source code and editor buffers; EMQX touches IoT data. The profiles do not show a specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch, so only a low compliance concern is supportable. The other agent is cited because the risk is about cross-system handling of different data classes, but no concrete breach is documented.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is copied into Continue-managed files
IF retention or residency rules differ between the two systems
mitigations: Classify data before sharing
Keep regulated data out of the IDE workspace
Document retention settings for both systems
Review access logs weekly
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
